title: The services page a small consultancy actually needs
metaTitle: The services page a small consultancy needs
excerpt: Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a working session. Say what the buyer stops doing themselves. A grid of capabilities does not make that comparison.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, a small set of distinct pieces rather than a wall of identical options.
caption: A few distinct pieces are easier to choose than a rail of sameness. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should each consultancy service block contain?
faqs.answer: Write an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The outcome is what the buyer holds when you stop. The boundary is the work you will not do, including the rollout they still own. The next step is a working session on that problem, not a general contact link.

faqs.question: How many services should a small consultancy list?
faqs.answer: Most firms should show two or three problems they want to be hired for. One honest offer is stronger than six tiles. Remove paused work. Group two problems only when the session, the fee shape, and the refusal are the same.

faqs.question: How should the page talk about doing the work in-house?
faqs.answer: Say what they stop doing, what they still do, and what goes wrong if they postpone the decision. Do not insult the in-house attempt. They often know the customers better than you do. Your offer is the decision they have been avoiding.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small consultancy services page should list the work in the buyer's language. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to book a working session. A grid of vague capabilities does not help someone who is comparing you with doing it themselves. They already have capabilities. They are stuck on a decision. Google's people-first guidance asks whether a reader leaves knowing enough to act. "Advisory, facilitation, and strategy" does not answer that. A named problem does.

Write one block per problem you want to be hired for. If you cannot say what is finished, what you will not do, and how the session starts, it is not an offer. It is a heading waiting for a meaning.

## Outcome, boundary, and the session

Treat every offer as three sentences.

The outcome is what they hold when you stop. A price list they can send. A weekly cadence the founder is no longer required to attend. A homepage sentence a stranger can repeat. Not "clarity." Clarity is the feeling. The artifact is the outcome.

The boundary is where they go back to doing it themselves, on purpose. You do not run the rollout. You do not hire their staff. You do not stay for the quarter unless a different offer says so. A buyer comparing you with their own time is looking for the edge, because an edge is what makes hiring you finite. An offer without an edge looks like a job they cannot quit.

The next step is the working session for that problem. The link should say "Book a session on pricing," and it should carry the problem into the scheduler or the form. One "contact" link under eight tiles throws them into a general inbox. They already told you the problem by choosing the block.

If a block cannot hold the three sentences, cut the offer until it can. A shorter list of real problems beats a complete-looking menu. Nielsen Norman Group's finding is the editing rule: on a typical visit people have time to read only about a quarter of the words, and the visit lasts a little less than a minute. They will not infer your offer from a grid in that minute.

## Use the words they use when they complain

Internal names are a common failure. The firm says "fractional leadership," "transformation," and "strategic partner." The buyer says "I am still in every deal" or "we do not know what to charge." The page should use the second set.

Read the last ten inquiries. Circle the nouns they used before you translated them into your method. Those nouns are the headings. The method can sit in the boundary. The method should not be the heading. They did not come to buy a method. They came to stop doing a job they are bad at or tired of.

A few swaps:

- "Strategy" should become the decision, such as which offer to stop selling.
- "Workshops" should say what is decided in the room, and that a workshop with no decision is not this offer.
- "Coaching" should say who is coached and what they will do differently the next morning.
- "Research" should say it is an input, not the decision, so nobody books it expecting the price list.

Do not add a glossary that translates your brand words back into plain words. Use the plain words as the headings. The brand can live in the sound of the sentences.

## The line about doing it themselves

Each block should contain one sentence a DIY buyer can use. What they stop doing. What they still do. What goes wrong if they keep doing it alone for another quarter. That sentence is not a scare. It is the comparison they are already running.

"You stop rewriting the quote for every deal. You still approve exceptions. If you keep rewriting them yourself, the price list will exist and nobody will use it." That is a fair comparison. "Unlock your potential" is not a comparison. It asks them to feel something. They were trying to decide something.

Do not insult the in-house attempt. They are often right that they know the customers better than you do. Your offer is the decision they have postponed, not a claim that you know their business. Write it that way. Respect is part of the boundary. Arrogance sends them back to the spreadsheet, which they at least control.

If the honest sentence is "you could do this yourself in a week if you would sit still," say that, and say why the session is the sitting still. Some of the best offers are a forced hour, not a mystical expertise. A buyer comparing you with themselves will trust that more than a claim of secret knowledge.

## How many offers belong on the page

Most small firms should show two or three problems. More than that and the page becomes the industry list in disguise, a directory of everything you have tried. One problem, written with a boundary, is a stronger page than six tiles.

Group only when the buyer would group them. Pricing and packaging can share a block if the session, the fee shape, and the refusal are the same. Do not group "pricing" and "hiring" because both are "hard." The buyer has one stuck thing.

Give each offer the same structure. Heading. Outcome. Boundary. The DIY line. The session link. Resist a special layout for the offer you are most proud of. Pride is not a reading order. If an offer is paused, remove it. A services page is a promise of current work. An old offer collects sessions you will decline.

## What a capability grid wastes

A grid of icons fails this buyer in a specific way. Each cell is a noun with no edge. Research. Workshops. Stakeholder interviews. Change management. The cells describe activities they could assign to themselves. The grid spends the page on your process instead of on their decision. An interview is not an outcome. A decision they can send is an outcome.

Replace the grid with the three-sentence blocks. A person who reads only the headings should know which problem is theirs. If the headings are "Discover, Design, Deliver," they cannot. Those words describe your week. They do not describe their stuck Tuesday.

Keep one sentence for what you refuse across all offers. No open-ended retainer disguised as a project. No session without the person who can say yes. No second problem slipped into the same fee. That sentence does more than a row of capabilities, because it is a decision about the relationship.

## Order the page the way a session happens

Open with the problem you most want a DIY buyer to recognize. Not the largest fee. Not the work that is easiest to staff. The one that matches the sentence on the homepage. If the homepage says pricing, the first block should be pricing, written out, not a teaser back to the homepage.

Then the problems that are easy to confuse with it. A one-session decision next to a project that implements it, so the boundary is visible. A diagnostic next to the decision, so nobody pays for notes and expects the price list.

End with the session, repeated, and a line on what to bring. The postponed decision. The person who can say yes. The artifact they have already attempted, even if it embarrasses them. You do not need their whole history to know whether you should meet.

Do not bury the fee in every block if the pricing page holds the shape. One line is enough. The services page has to stand alone for the visitor who never saw the homepage. They should still see the outcome, the edge, and the session.

## A block you can draft this week

Sit with one live problem and write the block in a document, not in a design tool.

Heading: the stuck thing, in their complaint.
Outcome: what they hold, with a form if you use one.
Boundary: two things you will not do.
DIY line: what they stop, what they still do.
Action: book a session on this problem.

Read it to the person who does the work. If they say you also do many other things, do not add those things to the block. Another block, or off the site. The block is a door, not a biography of the practice. If the door needs a footnote to make sense, the heading is still in your vocabulary. Rewrite the heading before you add the footnote.

When the blocks are true, the page stops being a menu of capabilities. The about page can then name who will be in the room. Read [who should be named, and why the origin story usually should not](/blog/how-a-small-consultancy-should-write-an-about-page) once the offers are specific enough that a stranger would care who shows up.

If you want help turning a list of capabilities into offers with edges, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The pattern to borrow is a page that could not be about a different problem.
